note: Open software, models and data for glass, placed by the job each does and by how it can be used on a web page. Licenses and last-commit dates were read from each project's own repository or page on the checked date. 'here' says how this site uses it.

routes.name: Runs in a web page
routes.sub: Small enough to run in the browser, and licensed so it can ship with a page.

routes.name: Run offline, publish the results
routes.sub: Too large for a page, or GPL code: run it once and publish the numbers it gives.

routes.name: Desktop tool or test aid
routes.sub: Used to generate or check numbers; not part of a page.

routes.name: Paid or restricted
routes.sub: Behind a fee or a login, or there is nothing to download.

gaps.title: Color from composition
gaps.text: No open model predicts the color of a glass from its oxides and redox state. This site's spectral engine is a partial attempt with illustrative and measured colorant curves.

gaps.title: Chemical durability
gaps.text: No open composition model for how fast a glass weathers. SciGlass has durability data, but not in its open text release.

gaps.title: Measured absorption spectra
gaps.text: Few are open. Most sit in papers as figures, or behind SciGlass Next's login.

tools.name: SciGlass
tools.by: EPAM Systems (2019 open release); plain-text conversion by Daniel R. Cassar
tools.license: ODbL 1.0 (the license file is headed ODbL)
tools.what: About 423,000 glasses from more than 40,000 papers and patents, each with its main-oxide composition and up to about 60 standard properties: viscosity points, density, index, expansion, Tg, liquidus.
tools.here: The oxide bench on the home page plots the nearest measured melts against its composition models.

tools.name: SciGlass Next
tools.by: Otto Schott Institute, University of Jena
tools.license: Original data ODbL; no license stated for additions
tools.what: A maintained web version of SciGlass with corrections since 2019, about 15,000 optical spectra, a property predictor, an API (key by request) and an MCP server.
tools.here: Not used yet. The spectra would replace drawn colorant curves.

tools.name: INTERGLAD
tools.what: A commercial glass property database that includes data published after 2019.
tools.here: Not used: readers could not follow the numbers back.

tools.name: refractiveindex.info
tools.what: Refractive index and extinction data with sources, for optical glasses, fluoride and chalcogenide glasses, metals and crystals, plus vendor glass catalogs.
tools.here: Source of the cited dispersion formulas in the Light Lab and the refraction stage.

tools.name: Glazy data
tools.what: 12,892 ceramic glaze records (2021 export) with oxide analysis, firing cone and kiln atmosphere. 12,035 carry a color sampled from photographs. A glaze is a glass fused onto clay.
tools.here: Planned: fired color against composition and redox, such as copper green in an oxidizing kiln and copper red in a reducing one. The colors come from photographs and would be labeled that way.

tools.name: Meulebroeck et al. 2016 spectra
tools.by: Wendy Meulebroeck, Hilde Wouters, Karin Nys and Hugo Thienpont
tools.what: Measured transmission spectra (300–1500 nm) of 85 panes from two stained-glass panels: cobalt blues, chromium greens, iron yellows, copper rubies and silver stain. Each curve is normalized, with no thickness given.
tools.here: The cobalt, chromium and silver curves on this site are traced from it, for their shapes.

tools.name: DiSCoMaT
tools.what: A model that extracts composition tables from glass papers.
tools.here: Not used: SciGlass already holds the compositions this site needs.

tools.name: Fluegel, Young & Finn, Appen models
tools.by: Alexander Fluegel (2007–2008); Young and Finn (1940); A. A. Appen
tools.what: Composition models fitted to measured glasses: viscosity at fixed points, refractive index and dispersion, density, thermal expansion.
tools.here: Drive the oxide bench. Within soda-lime glass the viscosity model misses SciGlass measurements by about 10 °C (median).

tools.name: GlassNet
tools.by: Daniel R. Cassar (2023), in the GlassPy package
tools.license: GPL-3.0 or later, code and weights
tools.what: A neural network trained on SciGlass that predicts 85 properties from composition, including liquidus temperature, Tg, elastic moduli and crystallization temperatures. The weights are a 127 MB download.
tools.here: Planned as a second prediction beside the fitted models, and for liquidus, which sets how close a glass is to crystallizing at its working temperature.

tools.name: VITRIFY
tools.by: Carvalho, Loponi and Cassar (2026, in review), in GlassPy
tools.what: A classifier that gives the probability that a composition forms a glass on cooling.
tools.here: Not used yet. A probability map could be drawn over measured glass-forming regions.

tools.name: mlglass
tools.what: Earlier machine-learning models for Tg and other properties. Last updated 2021.
tools.here: Not used: GlassNet covers the same ground with more properties.

tools.name: PyGGi
tools.what: A web application with trained property models and a composition optimizer.
tools.here: Not used: there is no downloadable model to cite or run.

tools.name: NBS 710 viscosity
tools.by: Napolitano and Hawkins (1964), National Bureau of Standards
tools.what: The viscosity of one standard soda-lime glass, measured at eight laboratories from the melt to the strain point.
tools.here: The viscosity curve and fixed points on the home page.

tools.name: ViscNet
tools.what: A small neural network (about 16,000 parameters) that predicts three parameters of the MYEGA viscosity equation from composition: high-temperature viscosity, Tg and fragility. Every curve it gives therefore has the physical shape of a viscosity curve.
tools.here: Planned for fragility: why some glasses stay workable over a wide temperature range and others stiffen quickly.

tools.name: MYEGA and VFT equations
tools.by: Mauro, Yue, Ellison, Gupta and Allan (2009); Vogel, Fulcher, Tammann (1921–26)
tools.what: Short equations for how viscosity changes with temperature.
tools.here: The VFT equation drives the Forming Lab.

tools.name: GRD magma viscosity model
tools.by: Giordano, Russell and Dingwell (2008); Python port by M. O. Chevrel
tools.what: Viscosity of dry and water-bearing natural silicate melts from composition.
tools.here: Planned for obsidian and pumice: a few percent of dissolved water lowers the viscosity of a rhyolite melt by orders of magnitude.

tools.name: StatMechGlass
tools.by: Mikkel S. Bødker and others (2022), Aalborg University
tools.what: A statistical-mechanics model of short-range order. It predicts how many network formers carry 4, 3, 2, 1 or 0 bridging oxygens (the Qⁿ distribution) from composition, with fitted values for silicate, borate and phosphate systems.
tools.here: Planned for the oxide bench, to show how adding Na₂O breaks the silica network and why viscosity falls.

tools.name: SHIK, Pedone and DeePMD potentials
tools.by: Sundararaman, Huang, Ispas and Kob (SHIK); Pedone and others (2006); Bertani and others (2024)
tools.what: Interatomic potentials fitted for oxide glasses, for molecular dynamics in LAMMPS. The DeePMD one is a machine-learned potential for sodium silicates.
tools.here: Planned: one offline simulation of silica and a sodium silicate, published as atom positions for a 3D view.

tools.name: LAMMPS and Atomify
tools.what: The standard molecular dynamics engine, and a browser build of it. The browser build needs cross-origin isolation headers that many static hosts cannot set.
tools.here: The engine for the offline simulation. Atomify is better linked to than embedded.

tools.name: R.I.N.G.S.
tools.by: Sébastien Le Roux and Philippe Jund
tools.what: Ring statistics and other structure analysis for atomic networks.
tools.here: Analysis for the offline simulation.

tools.name: Structure Lab engine
tools.what: A two-dimensional molecular dynamics model in the browser.
tools.here: Shows how cooling rate decides between a crystal and a glass.

tools.name: Spectral color engine
tools.what: Transmission spectrum × lamp spectrum × CIE 1931 2° observer, adapted to D65 and encoded as sRGB, with Beer–Lambert mixing and thermal glow from Kirchhoff's law.
tools.here: Computes the colors on the site.

tools.name: Mie theory with gold and silver optical data
tools.by: Johnson and Christy (1972) optical constants, via refractiveindex.info
tools.what: Absorption and scattering by metal nanoparticles in glass, from measured optical constants.
tools.here: Planned to compute gold ruby, silver yellow and the Lycurgus Cup's two colors. The heat-treatment sliders use hand-picked colors until then.

tools.name: miepython
tools.what: Mie scattering calculations in Python.
tools.here: Reference values to test the browser Mie code against.

tools.name: colour-science
tools.what: A Python library for colorimetry: color matching functions, illuminants, chromatic adaptation and color spaces.
tools.here: Reference values to test the spectral engine against.

tools.name: ray-optics and opticalglass
tools.what: Lens design in Python, with readers for the Schott, Ohara, Hoya and other optical glass catalogs.
tools.here: Not used: the Light Lab takes its indices from cited dispersion formulas.

tools.name: Tantalum
tools.what: A spectral two-dimensional light transport renderer in WebGL.
tools.here: A reference for the Light Lab's ray tracer.

tools.name: Mitsuba 3
tools.what: A spectral, physically based 3D renderer.
tools.here: Not used: it runs on the desktop only.

tools.name: Forming Lab engine
tools.what: A gather of hot glass on a blowpipe: viscous flow, sag and radiative cooling.
tools.here: The Forming Lab.

tools.name: Tool–Narayanaswamy–Moynihan model
tools.what: Structural relaxation through the glass transition, using fictive temperature. It explains why cooling rate changes a glass's density and stress.
tools.here: Not used yet. Short enough to write for the annealing stage.

tools.name: OpenGlaze
tools.what: A ceramic glaze calculator and recipe manager.
tools.here: Not used: the oxide bench already converts recipes to oxides.
